Within 6 months of the termination of the stressor or its consequences

S081.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
S081.description: Emotional or behavioral symptoms appearing in response to an identifiable stressor.

subtypes.With Depressed Mood: Symptoms mainly include low mood, tearfulness, or feelings of hopelessness.
subtypes.With Anxiety: Symptoms mainly include nervousness, worry, jitteriness, or separation anxiety.
subtypes.With Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood: A combination of depression and anxiety symptoms appears.
subtypes.With Disturbance of Conduct: Symptoms mainly involve violation of rules, truancy, vandalism, reckless driving, or fighting.
subtypes.With Mixed Disturbance of Emotions and C: Both emotional symptoms (depression, anxiety) and behavioral problems appear together.
subtypes.Unspecified: Maladaptive reactions not classified into the above types (e.g., physical complaints, social withdrawal).

symptom.disease_info: Adjustment Disorder is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms within three months of an identifiable stressor, with distress that is out of proportion to the stressor or associated with significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. The presentation can include anxious, depressed, or mixed mood changes, as well as maladaptive behaviors, but does not meet full criteria for another specific mental disorder and is not merely an exacerbation of a preexisting condition. Symptoms typically resolve within six months after the stressor or its consequences have ended, though it can become chronic if the stressor persists. It is differentiated from normal stress reactions by the degree of impairment and from disorders such as major depressive disorder or generalized anxiety disorder by its time-limited course and clear temporal relationship to a specific stressor.

patient.personality: Gary is a methodical, data-driven problem solver who values balance, quiet reflection, and cooperative relationships in both work and home life.
patient.stressor: Roughly two and a half months ago, Gary’s spouse disclosed that they were seriously considering a trial separation after a series of unresolved disagreements about starting a family and Gary’s long work hours on a major organizational restructuring project. Accustomed to approaching problems analytically, he initially threw himself into reading relationship books and tracking "metrics" of their communication, trying to negotiate solutions while still meeting high expectations at work. As the weeks went on and his spouse began spending more nights away at a friend’s place, the uncertainty at home started to bleed into his normally steady performance; he found himself second-guessing decisions, avoiding social board game nights with friends, and skipping outings like Red Rock hikes that had previously grounded him. When his supervisor gently noted a drop in his engagement and his spouse suggested counseling as a condition for reconsidering the relationship, Gary recognized that his usual self-reliant coping strategies were no longer sufficient and sought psychiatric evaluation to better manage his reaction to the relationship crisis.
patient.chief_complaint: Ever since my marriage hit this rough patch, I’m reacting to the stress in ways that don’t feel like me and it’s starting to affect my work and home life.

S081.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
S081.description: Emotional or behavioral symptoms appearing in response to an identifiable stressor.
S081.manifestation: Ever since my wife brought up the trial separation, I’ve been swinging between feeling panicky that the marriage is about to collapse and then just flat and hopeless, and I catch myself doing things that are totally unlike me—like zoning out at work, avoiding friends, and obsessively tracking our text exchanges in a spreadsheet—as if I can somehow calculate my way out of this, even though it’s clearly making everything in my life run worse.
